title: An AI Arbitrator? The Latest Innovations from the American Arbitration Association, with CEO Bridget McCormack and CTO Diana Didia
author: Bridget McCormack · Diana Didia

kp.k: AI arbitrator begins with opt-in construction disputes
kp.d: McCormack describes a November 3rd launch for documents-only construction disputes, chosen because parties need speedy resolution and AAA already has a regularly used documents-only process and domain expertise. Didia says participation will be entirely opt-in. At the interview date, testing used completed-case simulations rather than actual live disputes, and early-adopter recruitment remained the next step.
qs: Documents only construction cases.
And so that is the first AI arbitrator that will be uh live November 3rd.
But we haven't had actual cases go through it.
And we are, uh yeah, it is all opt-in, all an opt-in process.

kp.k: Human arbitrators verify, edit, and issue AI-drafted awards
kp.d: Didia describes AI-generated case summaries, document timelines, claims and issue analysis, and a draft award. The human arbitrator examines the award and evidence, can edit the result, and certifies and issues it in their own name. The transcript expressly corrects the suggestion that AI issues the award: the current design retains human responsibility rather than relying directly on autonomous output.
qs: It shows them the claims and issue analysis, but the piece that is different is it actually drafts an award.
And now the human arbitrator is spending time uh reading that award and looking at the evidence.
and it's actually their name, it's their award that they're issuing in the end.
The AI is drafting an award, but the human is issuing it, I think is what you mean. But yes.

kp.k: Parties verify AI interpretations before adjudication
kp.d: Didia and McCormack describe a preliminary verification stage in which parties confirm or correct the system’s reconstruction of claims, elements, supporting evidence, and legal frameworks before an arbitrator is appointed. Corrections feed back into the AI engines. McCormack argues this could prevent misunderstandings that parties otherwise discover only after a decision, and improve their sense of being heard.
qs: The AI is very transparent, is breaking out all of their claims and that is actually validated.
And the filers are able to confirm that or edit it.
Only at the point when all the submissions are in is an arbitrator appointed to the case.
it's showing all the different claims, each element of a claim, what evidence it believes you think supports that claim, and the legal framework surrounding that claim.

kp.k: Proprietary cases and specialist expertise underpin development
kp.d: McCormack says AAA trained the first version on over 1500 domain-specific cases and involved construction arbitrators throughout development and testing. Didia identifies diverse issues, photographs and other evidence, and reasoned human awards as important assets: awards serve as benchmarks and help map human decision-making for emulation. She separately reports simulations involving over thousand completed cases, with arbitrators, lawyers, and law students playing the participants; the transcript supplies no numerical accuracy results.
qs: we were able to train this first version of our AI arbitrator on over 1500 cases that are, are, you know, domain specific.
Our moat doing all this is that we have the cases and the human issued awards to use as benchmarking against the AI arbitrator's output
And then we've had arbitrators, lawyers, law school students all play the claimant and the respondent and the arbitrator.
And we've done that with over thousand cases.

kp.k: Efficiency claims combine participant reports and projected savings
kp.d: Didia reports that participating arbitrators said case-material review was about 30 to 50 % faster with AI organisation and a proposed outcome. Separately, McCormack reports team calculations against the legacy documents-only construction process projecting 30 to 50 % initial cost savings and 25 to 30 % initial time savings. These are not presented as live deployment results. Her expectation of progressively faster and cheaper service is a forecast.
qs: they are reviewing those case materials about 30 to 50 % faster than they would without the AI having done all that work and having not proposed an outcome.
We think the cost savings are gonna be anywhere from 30 to 50 % just at the start.
And the time savings are 25 to 30 % at the start.
It's only gonna, the time is only gonna get faster and the cost is only gonna come down.

kp.k: Autonomous awards remain a possible future option
kp.d: McCormack asserts that Didia would regard the technology as capable of issuing awards with accuracy and reliability comparable to most humans, while distinguishing technical capability from party and market readiness. She says the system is designed to permit removal of the human if users eventually want that. This is an attributed capability claim and conditional future direction, not an independently demonstrated outcome or current operating model.
qs: I think Diana would tell you right now that the technology is there for the AI to issue the award
But that doesn't mean that the market's ready for it or the parties are ready for it.
But it's designed so that the human can be unplugged one day if that's what the users want.

kp.d: McCormack attributes AAA’s progress to a pre-existing funded innovation programme, leadership support, organisation-wide training, and a structured idea pipeline. kp.d: Didia reports providing panelists with ClearBrief access and training when serving on AAA cases, and involving arbitrators in AI-arbitrator design. McCormack cautions that the community is diverse and anecdotally observes differing positions between in-house lawyers and their outside law firms.

kp.d: Didia identifies insurance payer-provider disputes as the next likely caseload because of volume, lower-dollar claims, anticipated interest in lower prices, and substantial data. These are development expectations, not demonstrated expansion results.

kp.k: Lower barriers could expand access and arbitrator demand
kp.d: McCormack predicts that cheaper, faster, simpler dispute resolution could expand AAA’s volume from half the million disputes annually to 10x that, rather than eliminate arbitrators’ businesses. She nevertheless expects business models to change and conditions continued opportunity on adapting to AI-native processes. Her access-to-justice argument concerns unresolved civil disputes and people, small and medium businesses, and organisations lacking resources to obtain legal help; the predicted demand expansion is not an observed result.
qs: I do think that their business models will change.

civil disputes, mostly because the barrier is finding legal help.
But if we can build this gate resolution that allows people to directly go figure out how to resolve their own disputes, that's a significant contribution to the broken civil justice market.

kp.k: Reusable agents could enable settlement and mediation products
kp.d: McCormack places AI mediation on the roadmap and predicts earlier understanding of dispute value could increase opportunities for human mediators. Didia says the arbitrator’s agents could be reconfigured through different workflows and interfaces into early case evaluation or settlement negotiation tools. Ambrogi’s suggestion that the arbitrator itself might prompt settlements is a proposed question to investigate, not a reported finding.

You could switch up the interface a bit and suddenly it would be an early case evaluation tool, something driving settlement.
For sure, you could just change the workflow, but the agents are still the agents.

kp.k: Procedural fairness motivates the party-feedback design
kp.d: McCormack invokes procedural-justice literature to argue that people who believe a court understood their complaints are more likely to accept adverse outcomes and participate in future proceedings. She connects that argument to AI’s capacity to make parties feel heard. The transcript cites no particular study or product-specific evidence demonstrating this effect, so the connection remains her rationale for the design.
qs: It's actually a robust literature that I'm sure you're aware of on procedural fairness, procedural justice.

are significantly more likely to accept an outcome that's adverse to what they wanted and then participate in the judicial process going forward because it's more about whether you're heard than what the outcome is.

kp.d: Didia identifies model-version upgrades after tuning, cybersecurity, continuing effectiveness monitoring, governance, and cost monitoring as emerging enterprise requirements. She predicts that maturing supporting tools will eventually enable sharply accelerating adoption, possibly after a quiet period. McCormack says AAA will retain traditional services for users who want them while iteratively improving new services through feedback, rather than requiring immediate market conversion.

or cybersecurity concerns, and all the different technology tools that will help us to monitor the ongoing effectiveness, the governance of the tool, the cost monitoring.
And I think it is going to get a little quiet for a while. And then that will be the hockey stick.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Didia describes an AI arbitration service that drafts reasoned awards while leaving verification, revision and issuance to a human arbitrator.
pts.d: The planned initial service covers documents-only construction disputes. AI deconstructs submissions for confirmation or correction by the filing parties, then presents an appointed arbitrator with summaries, evidence links, claims analysis and a draft award. The arbitrator reviews the evidence, may edit the draft and issues the award under their own name. This is human-verified adjudication, not autonomous issuance. McCormack nevertheless claims that technology could already support autonomous awards with human-comparable reliability and says the system is designed to permit removal of the human if users eventually want that.

pts.k: Didia and McCormack claim substantial review-efficiency gains and predict lower arbitration costs and shorter resolution times.
pts.d: Didia reports that participating arbitrators reviewed case materials 30–50% faster using the system. Separately, McCormack reports team estimates of 30–50% cost savings and 25–30% time savings against the legacy documents-only construction process at launch. These are distinct measures: reported review efficiency versus projected service-level savings. McCormack predicts further improvements as the technology develops.

pts.k: McCormack claims that party verification of AI's understanding can improve the dispute-resolution experience and procedural fairness.
pts.d: Before a draft award is generated, parties can inspect and correct the system's understanding of their claims, constituent elements, supporting evidence and legal framework. McCormack argues that this can address failures of human adjudicators to understand or respond to parties' arguments and make parties feel heard. She connects that mechanism to research on procedural justice, rather than reporting measured acceptance or fairness outcomes from the new service.

pts.k: McCormack predicts that cheaper, simpler AI-enabled dispute resolution will expand access and demand rather than eliminate arbitrators' businesses.
pts.d: She envisages resolving ten times AAA's stated current annual volume of roughly half a million disputes. Her argument is that lower cost, shorter duration and more direct self-service will bring previously unresolved civil disputes into a resolution process, benefiting people and resource-constrained businesses and organisations. She expects arbitrators' business models to change and makes continued career opportunity conditional on accommodating AI-native processes. The tenfold figure is an envisioned capacity or market expansion, not a reported result or dated forecast.

pts.k: McCormack and Didia predict a series of domain-specific arbitration products, with insurance disputes a likely next application.
pts.d: McCormack attributes the product's claimed advantage over a generic ChatGPT-based application to AAA's historical case data and arbitrator expertise. Didia identifies payer-provider insurance disputes as a likely next domain because they combine volume, lower-dollar claims, available data and anticipated demand for lower prices. Both expect subsequent applications to become faster to build; Didia also anticipates needing less additional domain data over time because foundation models already supply broad capabilities. These are expansion plans and capability expectations, not announced live services.

pts.k: Didia argues that substantial operational efficiencies require AI-native workflow redesign, not merely adding isolated tools.
pts.d: AAA plans to replace its case-management system by redesigning workflows from intake through award. Didia identifies hearing scheduling as a potential agentic task that could be introduced before the complete replacement. She also reports existing natural-language resources, document summary and Q&A functionality, and ongoing AI enhancements to panelist searches. The proposed change is therefore both automation of particular tasks and redesign of the enterprise process.

pts.k: McCormack predicts earlier settlement opportunities and more mediation work; Didia envisages reusing arbitration agents for case evaluation and negotiation.
pts.d: McCormack's stated personal view is that AI will give parties an earlier and better understanding of dispute value, revealing settlement windows sooner and increasing opportunities for mediators. Her comparison of one week with years or months is illustrative, not a measured timing improvement. Didia says the existing agents could be repackaged through different interfaces and workflows as early case evaluation or settlement negotiation tools, potentially as relatively quick follow-on products. AI mediation is on the roadmap, without a firm launch date.

pts.k: Didia reports demand for hybrid legal-technical roles, while both speakers describe organisational learning and collaboration as enablers of adoption.
pts.d: Didia says AAA has posted new roles combining legal and technical skills to translate subject-matter expertise into legal AI applications. She reports assigning about 20 staff full-time to the AI initiative, with applications exceeding available places by two or three times. McCormack credits a funded, structured innovation programme, staff access to technology and training with enabling development. Didia describes participating arbitrators as moving from binary concerns about AI toward practical questions about training and collaboration; these observations concern AAA's experience, not measured profession-wide attitudes.

pts.k: Didia predicts an eventual sharp acceleration in enterprise AI adoption as implementation and governance tools mature.
pts.d: Didia expects a quieter implementation period followed by rapid growth once enterprises assemble the required tools. She identifies model-upgrade governance, cybersecurity, effectiveness monitoring and cost monitoring as practical dependencies. McCormack distinguishes technical development from market readiness: AAA will continue traditional services while using feedback to improve AI-native offerings, without committing to when most users will adopt them.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists chiefly of AAA's historical data, simulations, participant feedback, internal calculations and leadership experience; broader market effects are predictions.
pts.d: McCormack reports training on more than 1,500 domain-specific cases. Didia describes using human-issued reasoned awards as benchmarks and simulations involving more than 1,000 completed cases, with arbitrators, lawyers and law students playing the participant roles. She explicitly says no actual cases had yet gone through the service. The 30–50% faster review figure comes from participating arbitrators' feedback; cost and overall time savings come from internal comparisons with the legacy process. No detailed measurement protocol, numerical accuracy benchmark or independent evaluation is supplied for the assertion of human-comparable autonomous decision reliability. McCormack invokes procedural-justice literature and her judicial experience, without identifying particular studies or reporting an AI-specific outcome study. Demand expansion, career growth, mediation growth and the enterprise adoption acceleration are expectations rather than demonstrated outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The first launch is scheduled for November 3 in the 2025 source; broader automation and adoption depend on user choice, suitable data and enterprise readiness.
pts.d: The construction product is announced rather than live at interview time, is entirely opt-in and retains a human arbitrator. Initial savings estimates concern that restricted use case at launch. The AI-native case-management replacement is planned within two years of the interview, independently of the autumn launch, with some components potentially deployed sooner. Insurance expansion and mediation or evaluation tools have no fixed dates. Autonomous award issuance is conditional on users wanting it, and AAA expects different customers to adopt at different speeds. Subsequent domain development depends on adequate, diverse data and customer interest. The tenfold dispute-volume aspiration and enterprise adoption 'hockey stick' have no specified deadlines.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern dispute parties, arbitrators and mediators, AAA staff, corporate legal buyers and people with unmet civil legal needs.
pts.d: Construction disputants are the initial users, with anticipated speed and price benefits and an opportunity to correct how their submissions are understood. High-volume insurance payer-provider disputants are prospective next users. Arbitrators move toward verifying AI-prepared analysis and awards, with McCormack predicting more demand but changed business models and a need to adapt. Mediators may receive more opportunities through earlier case valuation. AAA staff face workflow redesign and opportunities for project participation, while new roles combine technical and legal expertise. Corporate clients may select AI-led or predominantly human-led resolution according to dispute type; McCormack observes differing perceptions of opportunity and threat between in-house and external lawyers. Separately from enterprise savings, the access-to-justice prediction concerns individuals and resource-constrained businesses and organisations whose civil disputes currently go unresolved.
